The Minotaur. A hybrid creature with the head of a bull and the body of a man, imprisoned in an elaborate labyrinth on the island of Crete. His true name was Asterion, though he became known only as the bull-man after his transformation. He was the offspring of Pasiphae, wife of King Minos, and a sacred bull—the result of divine curse or punishment. The Labyrinth holding him was designed by the master craftsman Daedalus with such complexity that escape was impossible without magical aid.

He was neither fully man nor fully beast—he could not speak coherently and was driven by pure hunger. The Athenian tribute consisted of fourteen young men and women, sent every seven or nine years as food for the monster. The young hero Theseus ventured into the maze to end this shameful arrangement. Ariadne, the Cretan princess, gave Theseus a thread to navigate back through the Labyrinth after he killed the beast. The Minotaur's death marked the end of Athens' terrible obligation to Crete and freed the city from a terrible burden. Some versions describe him as being part of an unfinished prophecy, suggesting he might have been something greater had circumstances been different.
